summary:
The Accelerating Appraisals and Conservation Efforts Act (AACE Act), Public Law 118-230, enacted January 4, 2025 (originating as H.R. 5443), establishes a federal policy governing appraisal and valuation services for real property in transactions over which the Secretary of the Interior has jurisdiction. Section 2 is codified at 43 U.S.C. 1478; Section 1 (short title) appears as a note to 43 U.S.C. 1451.

The Act's operative mechanism (Section 2(a)) provides that a "covered appraiser"—defined in subsection (f)(1) as a State-licensed or -certified real property appraiser—need be licensed or certified in only one State to perform appraisal or valuation services in any State for a transaction within the Secretary's jurisdiction, thereby overriding State-specific licensure requirements for such federal transactions.

Subsection (b) governs the Secretary's use of non-Federal covered appraisers. It directs the Secretary, to the maximum extent practicable, to use a certified general real property appraiser licensed in the State where the subject property is located (paragraph (1)), and permits use of an out-of-State appraiser only upon the Secretary's determination that an in-State appraiser is unavailable within a reasonable period, not assignment qualified, or not cost competitive (paragraph (2)).

Subsection (d) contains statutory clarifications. Paragraph (1) preserves the application of other Federal and State laws and regulations to non-Federal covered appraisers, "except as provided in paragraph (3)." Paragraph (2) limits the new authority to transactions within the Secretary's jurisdiction, disclaiming any broader authorization to practice in a State where the appraiser is unlicensed. Paragraph (3) provides that any Federal or State law or regulation enacted before the date of enactment requiring State-specific licensure or certification shall not apply to transactions within the Secretary's jurisdiction.

Reporting obligations (subsection (c)): Not later than one year after enactment, and annually thereafter for at least the following four years, the Secretary must submit reports to Congress containing quantitative comparisons of appraisal-service request volumes and completion times (pre- and post-enactment), a qualitative assessment of subsection (a)'s flexibility, recommendations for congressional action, a workforce overview (including hiring, staffing, employees, and contractors), and a complete list of cases invoking the Act's authority with the specific criteria applied.

Subsection (e) imposes a 90-day deadline (after enactment) for making publicly available online, and upon request, all policies—including reference manuals, guidance, handbooks, standard operating procedures, and policy statements—governing the scoping, contracting, and review of Departmental appraisals.

Subsection (f) defines "Department" (Department of the Interior), "Secretary," "State" (including the District of Columbia and U.S. territories and possessions), and "reporting period" (the one-year period preceding report submission). The Act contains no appropriations.
